note: One round on the finished diff, dispatched with `kimi -p` and told to attack rather than confirm; it read scripts/board_seat_consumer.py, sentinel_lib/escalations.py, tg_notify.py and the two suites from disk itself. Findings accepted and fixed before this pack was written: (1) HIGH — the cap sliced rows[:max_rows] BEFORE filtering, and since foreign rows and families with no cure never leave the board and sort oldest-first, within weeks the whole cap would be spent on rows that were never curable while every curable row behind them went untouched (it named the starvation explicitly: 'permanent starvation... nothing behind them is ever attempted'); the cap now bounds cure ATTEMPTS, and zero-cost refusals do not consume it. (2) MEDIUM — the probe->close window: a condition that re-fires between open_seat_rows() and mark_resolved gets a fresh pending row, and a resolution written afterwards carries a newer ts and collapses the LIVE alarm into silence; the row is now re-read and must be unchanged before it closes. (3) MEDIUM — ts_epoch parses a naive ISO string as UTC, which in WITA is 8h into the future and enough to close a row whose run PRECEDED the alarm; a non-numeric state ts is now refused instead of parsed. (4) LOW — the dedup-key's job half was interpolated into a filesystem path, so `cron-fail:../..` read outside the state dir; the name is now validated. (5) LOW — mark_resolved's return value was discarded, so a row a peer closed first was still reported as this run's work. (6) LOW — the healer command-line probe was case-sensitive and a trampolined run carries HEALER_TRAMPOLINED. REJECTED, with evidence rather than argument: it called the machine field a CRITICAL mismatch, reasoning that the gateway writes rows through write_escalation (which stamps machine='pro'); the live e2e receipt in this pack shows tg_notify stamps machine=socket.gethostname() ('Air-M5' on the probe run), so the consumer's gethostname comparison matches. It flagged its own uncertainty on that one and asked to read tg_notify, which is why it is listed as a near-miss, not noise.

One round on the finished diff, `codex exec --sandbox read-only`. It did not reason about the code: it built an in-memory harness around the module and RAN eleven adversarial rows against commit bb6a5d0822, printing which ones came back 'resolved' and should not have. Verbatim from its run: 'invalid alert ts: resolved · boolean alert ts: resolved · foreign job and host: resolved · future clock: resolved · path escape: resolved · naive WITA time older than alert: resolved · pidfile race: removed replacement pid 9999 · empty successful ps: classified safe to remove · host collision: Pro resolution closes pending Mini job · board race: fresh failure closed with old proof · cap: recovered job starved behind 20 permanent rows — 11 assertions passed against bb6a5d0822; filesystem unchanged.' Every one was accepted. Six were already being fixed from the first seat's round; the two this seat found ALONE are now fixed and pinned: an empty-but-successful `ps` was being read as 'not a healer' and cleared a lock for a pid os.kill had just accepted (it is undecidable, and undecidable never cures); and a resolution is keyed on `job` alone, which every reader on this board collapses by, so closing Pro's `cron-fail:fly-pg-backup` would have silenced Mini's pending row of the same name — the locality guard protected the cure but not the resolution. It also established that mark_resolved returns 1 even when the job was already resolved (read_all_escalations filters resolved rows, so the original pending line is still found), which means the 'already_closed_by_a_peer' branch added in the previous round is near-dead code rather than the protection it was written as — recorded as a dissent rather than quietly dropped.
